verdict.rationale: Direct query of the lexical store grounds the verdict on both Testaments. In Greek, the verb 'to change one's mind, to repent' (metanoeo, G3340, 34 occurrences) and the noun 'repentance' (metanoia, G3341, 24 occurrences) recur across the Gospels, Acts, Paul, Hebrews, Peter and Revelation, and they sit inside the call to be saved rather than beside it. Mark 1:15 holds 'repent' (metanoeite) together with 'believe' (pisteuete) by the simple connector 'and' (kai). Acts 2:38 ties 'repent' (metanoesate) to forgiveness. Acts 17:30 universalizes the command. Luke 13:3 makes it the condition of not perishing. 2 Corinthians 7:10 marks the godly-grief 'repentance' (metanoia) as 'unto salvation' (eis soterian) and 'not to be regretted' (ametameleton). In the Old Testament the dominant turning verb 'to turn, to return' (shuv, H7725) occurs 1056 times across 38 books, concentrated in the prophetic summons to return, and 'to be sorry, to relent' (nacham, H5162) 108 times across 21 books. The bridge from the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint (LXX), in the store maps 'to turn' (shuv) to 'to turn back' (epistrepho, G1994) and 'to be sorry' (nacham) to 'to repent' (metanoeo, G3340) and 'to regret' (metamelomai, G3338), and Acts 3:19 and Acts 26:20 explicitly pair 'repent' (metanoeo) with 'turn back' (epistrepho), joining inward change of mind to outward turning. The pattern is dense, spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical), and stable, so repentance integral to conversion and bound to faith is well supported.

scripture.reasoning: Jesus opens his public proclamation with two present-tense commands held together by the simple connector 'and' (kai): 'repent and believe in the gospel' (metanoeite kai pisteuete en to euangelio). Direct query confirms both 'to repent' (metanoeo, G3340) and 'to believe' (pisteuo, G4100) stand in this verse. The two commands stand in the same breath, so repentance and faith are issued as a single summons rather than a sequence that could be split. The verb 'to repent' (metanoeo) names the change of mind demanded in response to the announced nearness of the reign of God.

Paul summarizes his testimony to Jews and Greeks as 'repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus' (metanoian eis theon kai pistin eis ton kyrion hemon Iesoun). Query confirms 'repentance' (metanoia, G3341) is present in the verse alongside the surface form of 'faith' (pistin). The single participle 'solemnly testifying' (diamartyromenos) governs both nouns, so 'repentance' (metanoia) and 'faith' (pistis) are the two coordinated objects of one act of solemn witness. The directional phrases, 'toward God' (eis theon) for repentance and 'toward Christ' (eis Christon) for faith, show the same conversion turning from sin toward God and resting on Christ as one movement.

Peter commands 'repent and turn back' (metanoesate kai epistrepsate), that your sins may be blotted out. Direct query confirms both 'to repent' (metanoeo, G3340) and 'to turn back' (epistrepho, G1994) occur in this verse. The pairing of the change-of-mind verb with the turning-back verb shows in the words themselves that biblical repentance is not bare mind-change but issues in a behavioral turn, which addresses directly the question of whether 'repentance' (metanoia) includes turning from sin.

Paul reports preaching that men should 'repent and turn to God' (metanoein kai epistrephein epi ton theon), doing 'deeds worthy of repentance' (axia tes metanoias erga). Query confirms 'repentance' (metanoia, G3341) and 'to turn back' (epistrepho, G1994) both present. Here the same 'repent' (metanoeo) plus 'turn back' (epistrepho) pairing recurs and is explicitly joined to corresponding deeds, so the lexical chain binds inward change, turning to God, and consequent conduct into one conversion.

Peter answers the convicted crowd with the aorist (a completed past action) command 'Repent' (Metanoesate), joined to baptism and tied to 'for the forgiveness of sins' (eis aphesin ton hamartion), with the promise of the Spirit. Query confirms 'to repent' (metanoeo, G3340) and 'forgiveness' (aphesis, G0859) present in the verse. The aorist (completed-action) form marks a decisive turn, and its placement at the head of the response to the question 'what shall we do' shows repentance as the entry response of saving conversion. The link to forgiveness sets repentance within the salvation event, not outside it.

Paul declares that God now 'commands all people everywhere to repent' (paraggellei tois anthropois pantas pantachou metanoein), the present infinitive 'to repent' (metanoein) as the universal demand replacing the prior times of ignorance. Query confirms 'to repent' (metanoeo, G3340) present in the verse. The scope marker 'all people everywhere' (pantas pantachou) makes repentance the required human response to God in the present age. This universalizes the call so that no class of hearer is exempt from the change of mind.

Paul contrasts 'godly grief' (he kata theon lype), which works 'repentance unto salvation that is not to be regretted' (metanoian eis soterian ametameleton), against the grief of the world that works death. Query confirms 'repentance' (metanoia, G3341), 'grief' (lype, G3077), 'not to be regretted' (ametameletos, G0278) and 'salvation' (soteria, G4991) all present in the verse. The phrase 'unto salvation' (eis soterian) explicitly ties the genuine 'repentance' (metanoia) to salvation, and 'not to be regretted' (ametameleton) signals a repentance that does not reverse itself. The grief that produces it is qualified 'according to God' (kata theon), oriented toward God, which matches the proposition that repentance is a turning toward God and not mere remorse over consequences.

Jesus warns 'unless you repent you will all likewise perish' (ean me metanoete pantes homoios apoleisthe), setting repentance as the dividing condition between perishing and not perishing. Query confirms 'to repent' (metanoeo, G3340) present in the verse. The present-tense subjunctive form in the 'if-then' clause (conditional) and the future 'you will perish' (apoleisthe) present repentance as the necessary turn that averts ruin. This places the change of mind at the heart of escaping judgment, integral to the saving response.

God declares that he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked but rather that the wicked 'turn from his way and live' (shuvu shuvu midarkekem haraim). Query confirms three tokens of 'to turn' (shuv, H7725) in this verse. The repeated command to turn, set against death and toward life, is the Old Testament engine of the conversion-turning idea, and the bridge from the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint (LXX), in the store maps this verb to 'to turn back' (epistrepho), the same verb Acts 3:19 and Acts 26:20 join to 'to repent' (metanoeo). The verse shows turning from sin and turning to God as the life-or-death summons.

Yahweh calls 'return to me with all your heart' (shuvu adai bekol levavkem), with fasting and weeping and mourning. Query confirms a token of 'to turn, to return' (shuv, H7725) here and in the following verse. The verb 'to return' (shuv) carries the directional turning toward God with the whole heart, and joins inward sorrow to a reorientation of life, the same coupling of grief and turning that 2 Corinthians 7:10 names godly grief producing repentance. This grounds repentance as wholehearted turning, not mere regret.

complicating_texts.resolution: The verse could be read to separate grief from repentance, but the text distinguishes worldly grief that produces death from godly grief that produces a saving and non-regretted 'repentance' (metanoia). The presence of the distinct word 'to regret' (metamelomai, G3338), used of Judas in Matthew 27:3, shows the canon has a separate word for mere remorse, which sharpens rather than weakens the claim that true 'repentance' (metanoia) is bound to salvation.

The phrase 'for forgiveness' (eis aphesin) has been read either as causal, repent in order to obtain forgiveness, or as result-based, repent because of forgiveness, but on either reading repentance is positioned inside the conversion event tied to forgiveness, so the inseparability of repentance from the saving response holds regardless of which sense of the preposition is adopted.

The proposition holds repentance and faith inseparable, yet here they are named as two coordinated objects, 'repentance' (metanoian) and 'faith' (pistin), which could be read as two distinct acts. The single governing participle 'solemnly testifying' (diamartyromenos) and the parallel directional phrases 'toward God' (eis theon) and 'toward Christ' (eis Christon) present them as two facets of one witnessed turning, so distinguishable in vocabulary but not separable in the conversion the words describe. The text does not rank one before the other, which is the locus of the remaining lens divergence noted in hermeneutics.

variants.note: The cited verses lie outside 3 John, the only book with examined CBGM (a method of tracing how New Testament manuscripts relate) data in this run, and the store reports no variant units bearing on 'to repent' (metanoeo), 'repentance' (metanoia), 'to turn back' (epistrepho) or 'to turn' (shuv) in these passages. The marginal sigla (apparatus markers) in the morphology surface forms of inputs.json reflect standard apparatus markers but none alter the presence of the repentance and turning words, which direct query confirmed in each verse.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that treats the Testaments as one unfolding call finds the Old Testament 'turn' (shuv) summons, 'return to me', mapped by the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint (LXX), onto 'to turn back' (epistrepho) and 'to repent' (metanoeo) and recapitulated in the apostolic command to repent and turn to God in Acts 3:19 and Acts 26:20, so repentance is the pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) turning that conversion completes, never separable from the faith that rests on Christ.

A reading that stresses repentance as turning from sin to submission finds direct lexical support in the 'repent' (metanoeo) plus 'turn back' (epistrepho) pairing of Acts 3:19 and Acts 26:20 and in 'deeds worthy of repentance' (axia tes metanoias erga), so the change of mind is inseparable from a turn of life and from faith in conversion.

A reading that defines repentance strictly as a change of mind about Christ rather than as a separate turning from sin can still affirm that 'repentance' (metanoia) is integral to conversion, since 'to repent' (metanoeo) lexically denotes a change of mind and Acts 20:21 names 'repentance' (metanoia) and 'faith' (pistis) as two facets of one message. It contests only whether turning from sin is a distinct condition added to faith, since the words coordinate the two without ranking them, and this is the genuine point the vocabulary leaves open.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the covenantal arc, so the primary method is redemptive-historical (reading the Bible as one unfolding story of salvation). Acts 20:21 and the 'repent' (metanoeo) plus 'turn back' (epistrepho) pairing in Acts 3:19 and Acts 26:20 are the controlling texts, joining inward change of mind to outward turning. The Old Testament 'turn' (shuv) pattern, 1056 occurrences across 38 books, and 'to be sorry' (nacham), 108 across 21, supply the pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) background, confirmed in the store through the bridge from the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint (LXX), of 'to turn' (shuv) to 'to turn back' (epistrepho) and 'to be sorry' (nacham) to 'to repent' (metanoeo) and 'to regret' (metamelomai). The one open question the words do not settle is the precise ordering and relation of repentance to faith, distinct condition, component of faith, or fruit, which the texts coordinate but do not rank.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine whether the lexical pattern of 'to repent' (metanoeo), 'repentance' (metanoia), and the Old Testament turning verbs presents repentance as occurring together with saving faith in conversion, or whether the terms appear in contexts that separate repentance from faith.
stem_audit.notes: The stem embeds an interpretive frame by calling repentance Spirit-given and never separable from saving faith, which preloads a conclusion about agency and inseparability. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form states the lexical question without the embedded verdict. The Spirit-given clause is a theological attribution not directly recoverable from the morphology of these verses, so it is treated as outside the lexical scope and left unscored. Confidence was raised from medium to high and pan_canonical from false to true after direct query established the Old Testament turning vocabulary, 'to turn' (shuv) 1056 occurrences across 38 books and 'to be sorry' (nacham) 108 across 21 books, and its bridge from the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint (LXX), to the Greek repentance and turning verbs, which the prior file lacked and had cited as its only reason for the lower rating.

lay_summary: The proposition says repentance is part of true conversion and cannot be split off from saving faith. The Greek words at issue are the verb 'to change one's mind, to repent' (metanoeo) and the noun 'repentance' (metanoia), and direct search of the word data confirms they occur 34 and 24 times spread across the Gospels, Acts, Paul, Hebrews, Peter and Revelation. Across the cited verses these words consistently sit inside the call to be saved rather than beside it. In Mark 1:15 Jesus issues two commands together, repent and believe in the gospel, joined by the simple connector 'and' (kai). In Acts 20:21 Paul sums up his message as repentance toward God and faith toward the Lord Jesus, both held under one grammatical frame. In Acts 3:19 and Acts 26:20 he tells hearers to repent and turn, placing the change-of-mind verb (metanoeo) next to a turning verb (epistrepho), which shows in the words themselves that repentance is not bare thinking but issues in a turn of life. In Acts 2:38 repentance is tied to forgiveness, in Acts 17:30 it is commanded to everyone everywhere, and in Luke 13:3 it is the condition for not perishing. In 2 Corinthians 7:10 godly grief produces a repentance leading to salvation that is never regretted, and the canon even keeps a separate word, 'to regret' (metamelomai), for mere remorse like that of Judas, so true repentance is marked off from regret. Crucially, the Old Testament supplies the same engine. The verb 'to turn, to return' (shuv), occurs over a thousand times across thirty eight books, thick in the prophets calling people to return to God, and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) renders it with the very turning word (epistrepho) the apostles use. So the pattern is not a New Testament novelty but runs through the whole canon. The one thing the words leave open is the exact order and relation of repentance to faith, whether a distinct step, a part of faith, or its fruit, since the texts pair them without ranking them. The core claim that repentance is integral to conversion and bound to faith is strongly and broadly supported.
